claims.text: Suppressing grain-boundary elemental segregation enhances the corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The enhanced corrosion resistance is caused by formation of a uniform protective oxide film.
The relevant conventional stainless steels contain passivating elements such as Cr and Ni and may contain minor Cu.
Controlled annealing can minimize grain-boundary segregation.
Adjusting alloy chemistry can minimize grain-boundary segregation.
A homogenized grain-boundary microstructure facilitates continuous formation of a coherent, slow-growing oxide layer.
Localized copper-rich grain-boundary regions or precipitates can act as deleterious corrosion sites in sulfuric acid.
Minimizing segregation prevents formation of copper-rich or other deleterious grain-boundary precipitates.
Reduced segregation produces a more even distribution of passivating elements.
An even distribution of passivating elements enables development of a protective oxide film.
The protective oxide film reduces localized anodic dissolution and impedes ingress of corrosive ions.
Samples processed to reduce segregation will have lower corrosion current density than conventionally processed samples.
Samples processed to reduce segregation will have more noble corrosion potentials than conventionally processed samples.
Samples processed to reduce segregation will have a more uniform passive-film morphology than conventionally processed samples.
Standard processing produces notable grain-boundary segregation that leads to discontinuous oxide films.
The proposed mechanism is limited to steels with adequate passivating-element levels under moderate corrosive and thermal conditions.
At very high irradiation doses or in highly aggressive chemistries, mechanisms other than segregation-controlled passivation may dominate.
A 0.5 M sulfuric-acid exposure at room temperature combined with electrochemical polarization can test corrosion behavior.
SEM-EDS measurements can compare oxide-film continuity and grain-boundary composition between treated and baseline samples.
Failure of segregation-suppressed samples to show statistically significant improvements in corrosion current, corrosion potential, and oxide-film uniformity would falsify the hypothesis.
